title: Myönsivät tehneensä virheen
subtitle: They admitted having made a mistake

blocks.text: Back in Lesson 16, virheistä, jotka myönsivät tehneensä sat only half-explained — you got jotka, but tehneensä was left alone. It's time to open it up. This is Finnish's compact alternative to että-clauses (Lesson 22): reporting what someone did or said, packed into one single word instead of two clauses.

blocks.translation: They admitted having made a mistake.

blocks.title: One word instead of a whole clause
blocks.text: Compare the two ways to say this: myönsivät, että he olivat tehneet virheen (with että, using the pluperfect from Lesson 24) versus myönsivät tehneensä virheen (compact, one word). Formal written Finnish — exactly the register of these reviews — often prefers the compact version. It reads as more polished, and it's everywhere once you know to look for it.

blocks.content: Take the past participle you already know (Lesson 3's -nut/-nyt), shift it to {-neen|grammar|referative suffix|having done (base form)}, then attach a possessive suffix (Lesson 14) matching whoever did the action. Tehdä → tehnyt → tehneen-, then + -sa/-nsä for 'they/he/she' → {tehneensä|grammar|referative construction|having done}.

items.en: They admitted having made a mistake.

items.fi: Hän kertoi {korjanneensa|grammar|referative construction, 3rd person|having fixed} auton itse.
items.en: She said she had fixed the car herself.

blocks.text: Piece 2 — Matching the possessive suffix to the subject

blocks.title: Same suffix family as Lesson 14
blocks.text: The ending after -neen isn't new — it's exactly Lesson 14's possessive suffix set, just doing a slightly different job. Tehneeni would be 'having done [by] me', tehneensä is 'having done [by] him/her/them'. Whoever is doing the admitting or reporting decides which suffix lands on the end.

items.en: I remember having paid too much.

items.fi: He kertoivat {korjanneensa|grammar|referative construction, 3rd person|having fixed} kaiken.
items.en: They said they had fixed everything.

blocks.text: Piece 3 — Reading it, not necessarily producing it fluently

blocks.content: This is a genuinely advanced structure — even the Paul Noble method doesn't expect you to produce it fluently on day one. The realistic goal here is recognition: when you meet a word ending in -neensa/-neeni/-neemme, you now know to look for the participle hiding at its start and the reported action it's carrying, rather than treating it as an unknown vocabulary item.

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Myönsivät tehneensä virheen, mutta eivät kantaneet vastuuta siitä.
lines.en: They admitted having made the mistake, but didn't take responsibility for it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Did they say they had fixed it for free?

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: They said so, but a bill came anyway.

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: You now have two ways to build the same idea, formal one-word (tehneensä) and plain two-clause (että olivat tehneet). Reading both is what matters most right now — reach for the että version when you're writing yourself, and simply recognise the compact version wherever it shows up in a review.

blocks.content: Tehneensä: TEH-neen-sä (three syllables, long held 'ee' in the middle). Korjanneensa: KOR-yan-neen-sa (four syllables — break it into kor-yan, neen, sa). Maksaneeni: MAK-sa-nee-ni (four even syllables, stress firmly on MAK).

blocks.title: What you now own
items: the -neen + possessive suffix shape, finally explaining Lesson 16's tehneensä
myönsivät tehneensä — admitted having done, a very common report structure in complaints
you can recognise this compact reported-speech shape and trace it back to the participle inside it
you understand it as a stylistic alternative to että-clauses (Lesson 22), not a wholly separate grammar
myönsi — admitted, a useful verb for reading disputed-responsibility reviews
